Jai Sharma · AI writing · Industry research

Flow matching and its descendants

What the field is. One regression and one target. The regression learns a velocity that carries one distribution to another, and its descendants change what moves (tokens, edits, molecules, and robot actions) and how many steps it takes, down to one for flow maps. The target is the base model tilted by exp(r/β), which reward fine-tuning, sampling from an energy, and QAM's critic-tilted robot policies all aim at, with stochastic optimal control as their shared math. Schrödinger bridges died as a general generator and live on inside samplers and control. MPC sits at an edge, since DIAL-MPC, its strongest result with roots in diffusion, learns no generative model. The other edges sit where neighboring fields check results their own way, physics by reweighting, weather by scoring rules, and molecule design by assays, and where rival programs such as drifting, regression policies, and parallel tempering win with no learned flow.

First principles

Every avenue on this page reuses one regression and aims at one target. The regression draws a simple path from each noise sample to a data sample and trains a network to predict the velocity along it. The network can only learn the average velocity at each point, and that average carries the whole noise distribution onto the whole data distribution. The target is the base model reweighted by exp(r/β). Each figure computes the real object for a toy target inside this page, so every claim in the text can be checked by moving a slider.

Figure 1 · the regression

Averaging crossing paths gives a flow

A network trained to predict the velocity along straight paths that cross learns their average, and the average is a flow whose paths never cross and still land on the data.

Pair each noise sample x₀, drawn from N(0, 1), with a data sample x₁ and move it along the straight line xₜ = (1 − t) x₀ + t x₁. A network trained by least squares to predict x₁ − x₀ from (xₜ, t) learns the average velocity through each point, uₜ(x) = E[x₁ − x₀ | xₜ = x], since the mean is what minimizes squared error.

Following uₜ from each noise sample gives paths that keep their order, so on the line they never cross, and the moving cloud has the same distribution at every t as the straight pairs. That second fact is the mimicking theorem Gyöngy proved in 1986, and it is why the regression works. Three groups published the method within a month in 2022, as flow matching, rectified flow, and stochastic interpolants.

Drag t or press Play. The shaded density is the same in both panels at every t, while the straight lines cross thousands of times and the flow paths never do. Near t = 0 every flow path heads toward the middle of the data, because u₀(x) = E[x₁] − x.

Unlocksevery avenue on this page. Flow Matching, Rectified Flow, stochastic interpolants.

Figure 2 · in space and time

The same flow in the plane, with time drawn upward

In two dimensions the straight pairs tangle, and the averaged flow bends so that no two samples are ever at the same place at the same time.

Each curve is one sample travelling from noise on the bottom plane (t = 0) to a five-cluster target on the top plane (t = 1). The flow commits each sample to a cluster early and then curves toward it, and that curvature is what makes sampling in a few steps hard (Figure 4).

Drag sideways to turn the scene, use tilt to look down the time axis, and switch between the pairs and the flow.

UnlocksFlow maps and one-step generation, which learn jumps along these curves, and Flow and diffusion models in control and Media generation and serving, which run the same flow over robot actions and video frames.

Figure 3 · couplings and bridges

Which noise goes to which data, and how much it wanders

Pairing noise with data by optimal transport straightens the paths, Brownian noise turns them into bridges, and the Schrödinger bridge sets both with one temperature ε.

Figure 1 paired noise and data at random. Entropic optimal transport pairs them to minimize E|x₁ − x₀|²/2 minus ε times the pairing's entropy, so as ε shrinks each noise sample goes to nearby data and the paths shorten. Letting each path wander like Brownian motion pinned at both ends, with variance ε t(1 − t), turns the lines into bridges.

With both set by the same ε the result is the Schrödinger bridge, the most likely way a cloud of Brownian particles could have travelled from one distribution to the other. Bridge matching learns the drift of that process between any two given distributions, such as unpaired image sets or snapshots of single cells over time.

Slide ε. Near 0.01 the pairs follow optimal transport and the paths run short and straight. Near 10 the pairing is close to random and the paths wander like diffusion.

UnlocksTransport between datasets and scientific inference, and optimal-transport pairing for straighter flows elsewhere. Diffusion Schrödinger Bridge, Diffusion Schrödinger Bridge Matching.

Figure 4 · one step

Few steps cut the corners of a curved flow

A flow takes many network calls to sample because its paths curve, and a flow map learns the jump from time s to time t so that one call can land where a path ends.

Euler's method follows the velocity in N straight steps, one network call each. With one step every sample lands on the data's mean, since at t = 0 the velocity points from each sample straight at E[x₁]. Consistency models, shortcut models, MeanFlow, and flow map matching all learn jumps along the flow instead of its instantaneous velocity.

Slide from 1 step to 64. The miss drops from 2.7 at one step to about 0.2 at eight and then halves with each doubling, and every step is a full pass of a large network.

UnlocksFlow maps and one-step generation, and the samplers behind Media generation and serving. Flow map matching, MeanFlow, continuous-time consistency models.

Figure 5 · discrete and edit flows

On tokens, velocities become jump rates

For text and other sequences each position switches from a source token to a data token at a random time, and the network learns the rate of each switch by the same averaging.

Masked diffusion starts every slot as a mask, so a fixed number of slots fill in one at a time and a short word needs padding. The network predicts, for each masked slot, the token it will become.

Edit Flows first align the source and the data with blanks, so each column keeps, substitutes, deletes, or inserts a token. Every column flips at its own random time, the sequence grows and shrinks as they do, and the network learns rates for insertion, deletion, and substitution.

Drag t. The masked row only fills slots that were already there, while the edit row deletes the A, turns the S into a G, and appends an E, so its length changes on the way.

UnlocksDiscrete, edit, and diffusion language models, and sequence design in Molecules, proteins, and materials. Discrete Flow Matching, Multiflow, MDLM, Edit Flows.

Figure 6 · the target

Reward fine-tuning has a closed-form answer

Maximizing expected reward minus β times the KL divergence from the base model p has one solution, p*(x) ∝ p(x) exp(r(x)/β).

Large β keeps the base model. As β falls, mass moves toward high reward, and in the limit onto the single best answer, which is where reward hacking starts. Reward fine-tuning, guidance, sampling from an energy, and extracting a policy from a critic all aim at this one distribution. On a space small enough to list, p* is a lookup, which is what a tilt test checks against.

Slide β. The bars are the three-answer toy: base probabilities 0.50, 0.30, and 0.20 with rewards 0, 1, and 2 become 0.18, 0.29, and 0.53 at β = 1.

UnlocksReward tilting, Learned sampling from unnormalized densities, which uses a negative energy as the reward, and Flow and diffusion models in control, which puts a learned critic in place of r. Tilt Matching.

Figure 7 · steering

Reaching the target means changing the dynamics

To sample p* from a pretrained flow, add (1 − t)/t · ∂ₓ log hₜ(x) to its velocity, where hₜ(x) = E[exp(r(x₁)/β) | xₜ = x] is the tilt a sample can still expect from where it stands.

The correction looks ahead: it averages exp(r/β) over every endpoint the base flow could still reach. This is Doob's h-transform, and every method in Reward tilting estimates h or its gradient. Adjoint Matching carries the reward's gradient back along each path, Tilt Matching avoids reward gradients, QAM puts a learned critic in place of r, and Adjoint Sampling uses a negative energy as the reward with simple noise as the base.

A common shortcut evaluates the reward at the denoised guess E[x₁ | xₜ] instead of averaging it. On this target the shortcut pushes samples past the tilted distribution, and Are we really tilting? shows reward guidance missing the tilt even for Gaussian targets.

Switch between the three and slide β. The exact correction lands on the target at every β. The plug-in shortcut overshoots, by about 0.6 at β = 0.5 and 1.2 at β = 0.2.

UnlocksReward tilting, Flow and diffusion models in control, and Learned sampling from unnormalized densities. Adjoint Matching, QAM.

Reward tilting

Probabilistic Inference in Language Models via Twisted Sequential Monte Carlo

Zhao et al. · 2024 · ICML 2024, best paper award

Casts steering a language model toward a sequence-level potential as sampling p₀·φ/Z with sequential Monte Carlo, learns twist functions that estimate each prefix's expected future potential with a contrastive loss, and bounds log Z from both sides so the gap between the bounds measures how far a sampler sits from its target.

A twist weighs each prefix as it grows

A twist scores each partial sequence by the potential it can still expect, so resampling can clone promising prefixes at every step and stop wasting particles on prefixes that will not reach the target.

The base model here is a Markov chain over three tokens, a, b, and c, run for 12 steps. The potential is a soft classifier on how many c tokens the finished sequence holds, φ = 1/(1 + e^(−2(count − 5.5))), so the target σ ∝ p₀·φ is a rare event. The base model writes six or more c tokens 1.6% of the time and the target 56% of the time. The exact twist, ψₜ(prefix) = E[φ | prefix] (the paper's Prop. 3.2), is a backward pass on this chain, the discrete version of the h-function in Figure 7.

Sixteen particles run the paper's Algorithm 1. At each step every particle extends its prefix with a token from the base model and takes the weight ψₜ/ψₜ₋₁, and the set is resampled in proportion to those weights. With no twist (ψ = 1) every weight before the last step is 1, so resampling only shuffles particles and all the information arrives with φ at the end. The learned twists come from the paper's contrastive twist learning, whose gradient is computed exactly on this toy, after 10 and 50 Adam steps.

Start with no twist and press Run again a few times. Most of the final weight lands on a handful of particles, and over 500 runs the effective sample size at the last step averages 3.8 of 16. Switch to the exact twist: weights now vary at every step, lineages that wrote few c tokens die early, and the last-step average rises to 13.6. The 10-step learned twist averages 5.1 and the 50-step one 12.8.

Two bounds on log Z close on the truth as particles grow

Running SMC gives a lower bound on log Z, running it again with one exact target sample planted among the particles gives an upper bound, and the gap between them caps the divergence between SMC's samples and the target in both directions.

The lower bound averages log Ẑ over ordinary runs of Algorithm 1. The upper bound averages it over runs of the paper's Algorithm 2, where one index carries an exact target sequence through every resampling step (Prop. 5.1). The gap upper-bounds the symmetrized KL divergence between the distribution of a sequence SMC returns and the target. On this toy the exact sequences come from the exact twist and log Z = −3.785 comes from the backward pass, so both bounds can be checked against the truth.

The twist-induced proposal draws each token in proportion to p₀·ψₜ, the variance-minimizing proposal of Prop. 3.3. With the exact twist every weight is then exactly 1, and both bounds equal log Z at every K.

With no twist and the base model as proposal the bounds sit 7.3 nats apart at one particle and still 0.45 apart at 256. Pick the exact twist and they come within 0.11 by K = 64. Then switch the proposal to twist-induced: the 50-step learned twist is within 0.14 at a single particle, and the exact twist closes the gap at every K.

Reward tilting

Are we really tilting? The mechanics of reward guidance in flow and diffusion models

Dandapanthula et al. · 2026 · arXiv

Shows that reward guidance which plugs a few posterior samples into the Doob h-function overshoots the reward-tilted target even for a Gaussian with a quadratic reward, and cannot move mass toward a distant high-reward mode. A closed-form damped reward scale fixes the first failure, and best-of-n sampling compensates for the second.

Plug-in guidance overshoots the tilt on a single Gaussian

Guidance that averages the reward's gradient over a few posterior draws pulls samples past the tilted mean and squeezes their spread, and on a Gaussian a damped reward scale removes the error at no extra cost.

The setting is the paper's Section 4.1: target N(0, 1), reward r(x) = −(x − a)² with a = 2, the tilt p·e^(λr), and the memoryless schedule. Exact guidance adds a correction built from ∇ log hₜ, where hₜ(x) = E[e^(λr(x₁)) | xₜ = x]. Most implementations instead draw k samples from p(x₁ | xₜ) and differentiate the log of their average weight e^(λr). As the step size shrinks this follows its expectation, a different flow for each k (Proposition 1). The figure runs 300 starts through 120 Euler steps with fresh draws at every step, for x up to 2.5.

With one draw the endpoint is Gaussian, its mean pulled √(πx)·e^(−x)·erfi(√x) of the way to a and its variance scaled by e^(−2x), where x = λσ². The tilt pulls 2x/(1 + 2x) of the way and scales the variance by 1/(1 + 2x) (Theorem 2). The plug-in pull passes 1 near x = 0.854, so the samples overshoot the reward's peak itself. Replacing λ with λₜ = λ/(1 + 2λσ²₁|ₜ) makes one-draw guidance exact for an isotropic Gaussian (Proposition 4).

At x = 1 one-draw plug-in samples end near 2.15, past the reward's peak at 2, with spread 0.37, against the tilt's 1.33 and 0.58. With 8 draws per step the mean falls to 1.48 and with 64 draws to 1.35, each step costing that many posterior samples. Damping with one draw lands on the tilt at every x. Slide x toward 2.25, where the one-draw pull peaks at 1.28.

Plug-in guidance cannot pick a mode, and best-of-n can

When the reward's gradient vanishes, plug-in guidance has nothing to follow and keeps the base model's mode weights, while exact guidance looks ahead to the mode a sample will reach, and keeping the best of n unguided samples recovers much of that.

The reward here is 0 above x = 1.3 and −R below it, on the page's three-bump mixture. Its gradient is zero almost everywhere, so plug-in guidance with any number of draws runs the unguided flow, the argument of the paper's Theorem 6, which states it for two symmetric bumps. Exact guidance uses hₜ(x) = 1 − (1 − e^(−λR))·P(x₁ < 1.3 | xₜ = x) from the mixture's posterior and bends paths toward the right bump from the first steps.

If p is the base model's share above the threshold, the exact tilt puts p/(p + (1 − p)e^(−λR)) there, plug-in guidance keeps p, and best-of-n gives 1 − (1 − p)ⁿ. Theorem 6 is the case p = 1/2, where best-of-n gives 1 − 2⁻ⁿ. Here p = 0.21.

At λR = 3 exact guidance puts 0.84 of the samples above the threshold, plug-in guidance keeps the base model's 0.21, and best-of-4 reaches 0.60. Raise n to 8 for 0.84 at eight times the samples. Raise λR and only exact guidance keeps following the tilt.

Reward tilting

Flow-GRPO: Training Flow Matching Models via Online RL

Liu et al. · 2025 · NeurIPS 2025

Brings online policy-gradient RL to flow models by swapping the deterministic sampler for an SDE with the same marginals, so each denoising step becomes a Gaussian policy with a log-density, and trains it with GRPO's group-relative advantages and a per-step KL. On SD3.5-M it reports GenEval rising from 63% to 95% and text rendering from 59% to 92%.

The SDE keeps the marginals and turns each step into a Gaussian policy

Adding noise at every step, with a drift that compensates for it, leaves the distribution at each time unchanged and gives every step a Gaussian transition with a log-density, which is what a policy gradient needs.

Flow-GRPO samples with xₜ₊Δₜ = xₜ + [v + (σₜ²/2t)(xₜ + (1 − t)v)]Δt + σₜ√Δt·ε and σₜ = a√(t/(1 − t)), in its own time where t = 1 is noise (eq. 9). The bracket rewrites the score through the velocity, so the SDE has the ODE's marginals at every time. The figure runs that update on the page's mixture with 10 or 40 uniform steps. The released code caps the noise at the first step, where σₜ is infinite, and the figure does the same.

Each of 24 samples in a group gets the page's reward r(x) = x and the advantage (r − group mean)/(group std), the paper's eq. 4. Every step of a sample is then pushed up or down by that one advantage through its Gaussian log-density. At a = 0 every step is deterministic and has no density to push.

At the default a = 0.7 the group spreads away from the dashed ODE paths, while the histogram of 2000 samples stays close to the base density, closer with 40 steps. Drop a to 0 and every sample follows its ODE path, and the marked step loses its Gaussian. With 10 steps at a = 0.7, 0.47 of the samples still end in the bump their ODE path reaches, against 0.37 if the start did not matter.

The noise level decides how much of the tilt the optimum reaches

Below a = √2, the σ² = 2η level that Adjoint Matching calls memoryless, the 10-step sampler keeps part of its starting noise, so the KL optimum it trains toward falls short of the tilt, and the ODE used for evaluation pushes the same model past it.

In continuous time every a > 0 forgets the starting noise, because the noise scale grows without bound at the noise end. Adjoint Matching's Proposition 1 counts all these schedules as memoryless, and its Theorem 1 adds that fine-tuning has to use a = √2 for the tuned model to sample the tilt under a different noise schedule, such as the ODE that Flow-GRPO's code uses for evaluation.

On a Gaussian with the mixture's mean and variance and the reward r(x) = x every step is affine, so the right panel is exact. With 10 steps the start noise survives: its squared correlation ψ with the end sample is 0.12 at a = 0.7, and the optimum of the paper's KL-regularized objective, sampled with those steps, moves the mean a share 1 − ψ of the tilt's move. Dandapanthula and Boffi derive the same under-correction for schedules that keep memory (their Appendix B.2). Sampled with the ODE in continuous time, the same optimal velocity moves the mean 4/(2 + a²) times as far as the tilt.

Slide a. The scatter starts as the ODE's monotone map at a = 0 and becomes a cloud near a = 1. At the default a = 0.7 the SDE optimum reaches 0.88 of the tilt's move and ODE sampling of the same model reaches 1.61, past the tilt. At a = √2 both reach 1.00.

Reward tilting

Reinforce Adjoint Matching: Scaling RL Post-Training of Diffusion and Flow-Matching Models

Bergmeister et al. · 2026 · arXiv

Shows that the KL-optimal process reweights clean samples and keeps pretraining's noising rule, so post-training becomes a regression on the model's own noised samples toward a reward-corrected target, with no SDE rollouts, adjoint solves, or reward gradients. On SD3.5-M it reports reaching Flow-GRPO's peak reward in up to 50 times fewer training steps, read from its training curves.

The optimal process only reweights endpoints

The best KL-regularized generator makes high-reward samples more likely and noises each sample exactly as pretraining does, so training states for the optimum can be made by noising the model's own samples.

The paper's Theorem 3.1 says a controlled process solves the KL-regularized problem exactly when its endpoints follow the tilt p·e^r/Z and its path, given the endpoint, has the reference law. The figure simulates 300 paths of the optimal controlled SDE on the page's mixture, with memoryless noise and the exact control (2(1 − t)/t)·∂ₓ log hₜ from the same closed-form h as Figure 7, and the reference SDE without control beside it.

Given its endpoint x₁, each state xₜ should then be t·x₁ plus (1 − t) times standard noise, the pretraining kernel. RAM's training loop rests on this: it draws an endpoint from the current model with an ODE sampler, scores it, and noises it K = 8 times, where earlier methods store an SDE rollout.

At temperature 1 the endpoint mean is 1.86 against the tilt's 1.85, and at t = 0.5 the fitted slope is 0.49 and the spread 0.51, against the kernel's 0.50 and 0.50. Lower the temperature and the endpoints crowd the right bump as the tilt does, while the dots stay in the band. Switch to the reference process: the endpoints return to the base mixture, and the band holds.

RAM's target uses the slope at the end of the tilt

The change the optimum makes to the velocity is the full rise of a path traced as the tilt grows from zero, RAM's regression target at the optimum supplies only that path's slope at its end, and the two agree on a Gaussian and differ wherever a noisy sample could still belong to more than one mode.

Tilt the endpoint law by e^(λx/β) with λ running from 0 to 1. The velocity u(λ) then moves with slope Cov(r, x₁ − x₀ | xₜ), which for r(x) = x/β is Var(x₁ | xₜ)/(β(1 − t)) on this page's time axis (the paper's eq. 19). The optimum needs u(1) − u(0), the integral of that slope (Lemma 4.2). RAM's fixed point, eq. 18, has the same form as the slope at λ = 1, so at the optimum its target asks for the end slope, and its first step from the pretrained model asks for the slope at λ = 0.

When the posterior of x₁ sits inside one Gaussian its variance does not depend on λ, the path is straight, and all three agree, the paper's Appendix B.4. On the mixture the tilt changes how the posterior splits between bumps, so the slope changes along the path. The paper notes that RAM and the KL optimum agree to first order in the reward.

At the default temperature 0.50 and t = 0.30, the probe at x = 0 needs a change of 3.59, while RAM's target at the optimum supplies 1.08 and its first step 6.24. Weighted by where tilted states sit, RAM's target misses by 73% at t = 0.2, 55% at t = 0.4, and 1% at t = 0.8, once a noisy sample has settled into one bump. Switch to the Gaussian and the three lines coincide.

Flow maps and one-step generation

Learning the integral of a diffusion model

Sander Dieleman · 2026 · Blog post

Sander Dieleman's survey treats a flow map as the integral of a diffusion model's velocity, one network that jumps between any two times of a path. It sorts the 21 methods in its summary table by the consistency rule each enforces (compositional, Lagrangian, or Eulerian), by whether it distills a teacher or trains from scratch, and by its cost per training step.

A flow map jumps between any two points of a path

A flow map takes a point at time s straight to where its path is at time t, the integral of the velocity that a sampler would otherwise add up in many small steps.

The post writes the map as F(x, s, t) = x + ∫ₛᵗ v dτ, the start plus the integral of the velocity along the path from s to t. A velocity model says which way to move next. The map says where the path will be at any other time, so one call replaces the whole integral.

Each blue chord joins one of six paths of Figure 2's flow at time s to the same path at time t. The dashed segment is one step of the velocity from s, which leaves along the tangent and misses (red), the corner-cutting of Figure 4. Jumps compose: two jumps through the midpoint land where one jump lands, the rule the post calls compositionality and others call the semigroup or shortcut property. With t below s the map runs back toward noise, so it is its own inverse.

This page keeps noise at t = 0 and data at t = 1. The post runs time the other way, as diffusion papers do.

Drag sideways to turn the scene and slide s and t. From s = 0 to t = 1, one velocity step misses by 2.65 on average while the jump lands on the path. With two jumps chosen, the two chords land within 1e-9 of the single jump, the solver's precision. Set t below s to jump back toward noise.

Each method trains a different slice of the same map

Flow-map methods learn the same two-time map from different sets of time pairs, and each ties a pair to its neighbors with one of three consistency rules.

The post's three rules each relate a jump to nearby jumps. Compositional: one jump equals two shorter ones. Lagrangian: as the end time moves, the landing point travels at the velocity. Eulerian: as the start slides along its path, the landing point stays put. The Lagrangian and Eulerian rules put a derivative of the network in the loss, computed with a Jacobian-vector product or a finite difference, and composition needs none.

The triangle on the right holds every pair of times (s, t) with s ≤ t, shaded by how far one velocity step from s lands from the path at t, averaged over 48 paths. That gap is what a flow map knows beyond the velocity. It is zero on the diagonal, where flow matching trains, and largest at the corner (0, 1), the one-step jump.

Consistency models train the top edge, jumps from every s straight to the data. Shortcut models train jumps whose lengths halve, drawn here down to 1/8, each matched to two half jumps. MeanFlow trains every pair by sliding the start, and Lagrangian self-distillation trains every pair by moving the end.

Switch methods. Trained on the diagonal alone, one call from this path's noise lands at −0.23, the data's mean, while the path ends at 1.87, and every slice that reaches the top edge lands at 1.87 once learned. The miss peaks at 1.42 at the one-step corner. The costs count a backward pass as two forward passes, so plain training costs 3.

Flow maps and one-step generation

How to build a consistency model: Learning flow maps via self-distillation

Boffi et al. · 2025 · NeurIPS 2025

Boffi, Albergo, and Vanden-Eijnden show that a map whose diagonal matches the velocity is the flow map exactly when it passes any one of three tests, and turn each test into a loss that trains a flow map from data with no teacher. Consistency models, shortcut models, and MeanFlow fall out as special cases, and the Lagrangian loss trains best in their experiments.

Three tests a flow map must pass, and the one that ties it to the data

Every flow map has to agree with itself and with the data: three equivalent tests check the first, and flow matching on the diagonal checks the second.

Boffi and coauthors write X(s, t, x) = x + (t − s) v(s, t, x), so on the diagonal s = t the slope v(t, t, x) is a velocity, trainable by flow matching (Eq. 6 and 7). Proposition 2.2 then gives three equivalent conditions for everything off the diagonal. Lagrangian: as the end time moves, the landing point travels at the map's own diagonal velocity. Eulerian: as the start slides along its path, the landing point stays put. Semigroup: two jumps land where one jump lands.

Each condition, squared, becomes a loss, LSD, ESD, or PSD, added to flow matching on the diagonal (Proposition 2.3). The two parts catch different errors. A blend of the exact map with one Euler step keeps the right diagonal and fails all three tests. The exact map of a velocity learned from shifted data passes all three tests, and only the diagonal test catches it.

LSD scores best in nearly every column of the paper's Table 1, with one-step CIFAR-10 FID 8.10 against 12.81 for PSD with midpoint splits. ESD, whose loss differentiates the network in space, became unstable on images and has no FID reported (Section 5).

Set the error to 0 and every readout is 0.000. At 0.5 toward one Euler step, the Lagrangian residual reads 0.394, the Eulerian 0.658, the semigroup 0.151, and the diagonal 0.000, and one-step samples miss by 0.794. With the wrong velocity and data shifted by 0.5, the three tests read 0.000, the diagonal reads 0.491, and samples miss by 0.500. Readouts are root mean squares over 96 draws made the way the paper's losses draw them.

Self-distillation spreads the diagonal to every jump

Trained from data pairs alone, a network learns the velocity on the diagonal by flow matching, and a self-distillation loss carries that accuracy to jumps of every length.

The network here has two hidden layers of 32 units and sees (x, s, t). Each training step draws 96 pairs for flow matching on the diagonal and 32 for the off-diagonal loss, three quarters of the batch on the diagonal as in the paper's experiments, with the stop-gradients of its Eq. 94 and without its learned loss weights. The derivatives LSD and ESD need come from forward-mode passes through the network, the Jacobian-vector products the paper computes with jvp.

Flow matching alone learns the diagonal and leaves the rest of the triangle to chance, so the error grows with the length of the jump and one-step samples miss the data. Any of the three losses brings the error off the diagonal down to the error on it.

The three losses end close together on this one-dimensional toy. The paper finds wider gaps, on its checkerboard and most of all on images, where ESD's spatial derivative made training unstable.

Press Train. After 6,000 steps with LSD the error off the diagonal is about 0.13, the same as on it, and one-step samples sit about 0.1 from the data in W₁, with the middle cluster the last to sharpen. With flow matching only, the diagonal reaches about 0.15 while the error off it stays near 0.4 and the samples sit about 0.7 away. ESD and PSD end at about 0.14 and 0.15 off the diagonal.

Flow maps and one-step generation

Mean Flows for One-step Generative Modeling

Geng et al. · 2025 · NeurIPS 2025, oral

Geng, Deng, Bai, Kolter, and He train one network on the average velocity over an interval, through an identity that ties it to the ordinary velocity, from scratch and with no teacher. It reports one-step FID 3.43 on ImageNet 256 (Table 2).

The average velocity over every interval of one path

MeanFlow's network learns u(s, t), the average velocity between two times, which equals the velocity when the interval shrinks to a point and gives a sample in one call when the interval runs from noise to data.

The average velocity from s to t points along the chord of a curved path, and the velocity at s points along its tangent. Over every pair s ≤ t, the average velocity of one path is a surface. Its diagonal is the velocity, which flow matching learns, and its corner (0, 1) is the one-step jump x₁ − x₀.

MeanFlow trains u through an identity derived from its definition (Eq. 6): u(s, t) = v(s) + (t − s) du/ds, with s the start of a jump, t its end, and du/ds the derivative as the start slides along its own path, v ∂u/∂x + ∂u/∂s. MeanFlow's own notation names the start t and the end r and runs time from data to noise, which changes the sign. It computes du/ds as one Jacobian-vector product, with tangent v in x and 1 in the start time.

Table 1b breaks this derivative on purpose. The one-step FID in its ablation setting is 61.06 with the derivative along the path, and the three wrong tangents give 268.06, 329.22, and 137.96.

At s = 0.20 and t = 0.85 on the right-hand path, u = 1.153, v = −0.499, and (t − s) du/ds = 1.652, so the identity holds to within 0.0001. The wrong derivatives move the target by −2.03, −0.99, and 1.04. Over 400 random pairs the identity's largest residual is 1.1e-5, while the wrong derivatives miss by 0.76, 0.50, and 0.52 in root mean square. One call with u from this path's noise lands on its end, 1.87, and one call with v lands at −0.23.

Pair velocities average out to the MeanFlow target

MeanFlow needs no teacher because its target is linear in the velocity, so the velocity of one data pair can stand in for the true velocity and the targets average to the right answer.

The velocity in the identity is an average over every pair (x₀, x₁) whose straight line passes through x at time s, the average Figure 1 computes. MeanFlow follows flow matching and puts one pair's velocity x₁ − x₀ in its place (Eq. 11). Each pair's target is then wrong, and their mean is still u: the target is linear in the velocity, and the stop-gradient holds everything else fixed, the argument Dieleman's post spells out.

The price is variance. Each pair's target is ∂X/∂x times its velocity plus a constant, so the targets spread ∂X/∂x times as widely as the velocities do. The stretch ∂X/∂x is largest on paths that end between clusters, where the flow map pulls neighbors apart.

Press Draw pairs. At s = 0.20 and t = 0.85 on the path into a cluster, after 20,000 pairs both running means sit within about one standard error of v = −0.50 and u = 1.15, errors of 0.01 and 0.02, though a single target has a standard deviation near 3.5. On the path between clusters the targets spread 6.52 times as widely as the velocities, so even after 20,000 pairs their mean carries a standard error of about 0.09.

Flow maps and one-step generation

Generative Modeling via Drifting

Deng et al. · 2026 · arXiv preprint

Deng, Li, Li, Du, and He train a one-step generator by moving its outputs along a field of attraction to data minus repulsion from other outputs, so the iteration a diffusion sampler runs at inference happens during training. Its field is computed in a pretrained encoder's features, and it reports FID 1.54 on ImageNet 256 in latent space and 1.61 in pixels.

Attraction to data minus repulsion from samples

Drifting moves each generated sample toward nearby data and away from nearby generated samples, and the two pulls cancel when the samples match the data.

Each pull is a mean shift: a kernel-weighted average of nearby data minus x, and the same over the other generated samples (Eq. 8 to 10). Their difference V is anti-symmetric, since swapping the data and the samples flips its sign, so V vanishes everywhere once the samples' distribution equals the data's (Proposition 3.1).

Eq. 2 moves samples by x ← x + V. The figure moves 256 free samples by half of V per step against 256 fresh data samples, with the paper's Laplace kernel exp(−|x − y|/τ) at τ = 0.5. Algorithm 2 in the paper adds a second normalization and sums three temperatures on normalized features, and one temperature on raw coordinates is enough here. Attraction alone drives each sample uphill to the nearest dense spot, and the paper's Table 1 measures the result: FID 177.14 with attraction only, against 8.46 with the anti-symmetric field.

The converse is open, as the paper says: a field can vanish without the distributions matching. Attraction alone shows the gap on this toy, ending near zero loss with every cluster collapsed.

Press Play from noise: within about 25 steps the samples settle onto the clusters and the loss falls from about 1.5 to about 0.004. Start from data and the field is already close to zero, about 0.003. With attraction only, start from data: the loss starts about 30 times higher, each cluster collapses to a point within 25 steps, and the loss then falls to about 0.001 anyway. The anti-symmetric cloud ends about 0.34 wide against the data's 0.28, a finite-sample bias that falls to 0.30 with 1,024 samples a side, in line with the paper's Table 2, where more positive and negative samples lower FID.

Training does the iterating, so sampling takes one call

A Drifting generator is a single network from noise to sample, and every training step moves its outputs a little along the drift.

The loss regresses each output f(ε) onto f(ε) + V with V held fixed (Eq. 6), so its value is the mean of |V|² and its gradient moves each output along its own drift. A network with two hidden layers of 32 units trains here with Adam on 256 noise draws and 256 fresh data samples per step, using the field of the figure above. The right panel shows its outputs for 512 fixed noise draws and the image of a grid drawn on the noise plane.

The grid shows the map itself. A continuous map cannot split one Gaussian cloud into five separate pieces, so the grid stretches across the gaps and some outputs land between clusters, the limit that a Lipschitz bound puts on any one-step map from a Gaussian (Salmona et al.).

Drifting computes its field in a pretrained encoder's features, and its authors report that the method did not work on ImageNet without one (Section 5.2). Raw coordinates are enough on this two-dimensional toy, as they were in the paper's robot-control experiments.

Press Train. Within a few hundred steps the outputs reach all five clusters, and by 2,400 steps each holds about a fifth of them, with about 8% between clusters against 1.1% for the data. Reset with attraction only and train: the clusters fill unevenly and one empties, while the loss ends as low as the anti-symmetric field's.

Discrete, edit, and diffusion language models

DiffusionGemma Technical Report

DiffusionGemma Team, Google DeepMind · 2026 · arXiv technical report

Google DeepMind fine-tunes Gemma 4 26B A4B, on under 10% of its training tokens, into a uniform-noise diffusion model that refines 256-token canvases and commits them one after another, at about 20 tokens per forward pass. It is the most complete public picture of where diffusion language models stand, including the concurrency at which the speed lead ends.

Tokens kept in the same pass are drawn as if independent

A pass draws the tokens it keeps independently of each other, so DiffusionGemma keeps adding the surest tokens only while the entropies of all but the last sum to at most a budget b, which caps the error one pass can add.

DiffusionGemma writes a reply in 256-token canvases, one after another, freezing each canvas before starting the next. A canvas starts as uniform random tokens, and every pass predicts a distribution for every position, sharpened by a temperature that falls from 0.8 to 0.4. Algorithm 1 ranks the positions by entropy, keeps a sample at the lowest-entropy ones, and puts fresh random tokens everywhere else. It keeps adding positions while the entropies of all but the last one added sum to at most b = 0.1.

Tokens kept in one pass are drawn from their own marginals. With an exact denoiser, the error that pass adds is their total correlation, the KL divergence from their joint distribution to the product of their marginals, and total correlation is at most the summed entropy minus the largest entropy, so the budget caps each pass's error at b. On this toy the denoiser is exact, computed from the toy's 30 sentences, and the temperature stays at 1. Positions not yet kept are blank to it, while DiffusionGemma's network has to recognize its fresh random tokens as noise.

Every pass computes every position of the canvas. DiffusionGemma averages 19.74 finished tokens per forward pass over a 256-token canvas, about 13 positions computed for each token it outputs, which costs little while one user's request leaves the GPU waiting on memory. Google measured the parent Gemma 4 with multi-token prediction overtaking it in total throughput at around 32 concurrent requests on one H100, before any tuning for large batches.

Each row is one pass, and the small numbers are entropies in nats. At the paper's b = 0.1 the first pass keeps the six fixed words and one city token, and each later pass keeps one uncertain token plus any that became certain: 2.72 tokens per pass, with the toy's distribution reproduced exactly. Switch to fixed k = 3 and the third pass keeps both halves of the first city at once, so 72.7% of sentences come out incoherent. Raise b to 0.7 and a second uncertain token joins a pass once the first has entropy ln 2 or less: 3.33 tokens per pass, still no incoherent sentence, KL 0.006.

Flow and diffusion models in control

Diffusion Policy: Visuomotor Policy Learning via Action Diffusion

Chi et al. · 2023 · RSS 2023, extended in IJRR 2024

Represents a visuomotor policy as a conditional denoising process over a chunk of future actions, run with a receding horizon. Two of its arguments are drawn here: a generative policy can represent demonstrations that solve a task two different ways, and committing to a chunk keeps consecutive actions on one of them.

Averaging two ways around drives into the obstacle

A least-squares policy outputs the average of demonstrations that pass an obstacle on either side, which runs straight into it, while a generative policy samples one side.

Each demonstration goes straight up, forks at y = 1, passes a disc on the left or the right, and rejoins. A policy trained by least squares to output the path from the start learns the mean of the demonstrated paths, since the mean is what minimizes squared error. With half the demonstrations on each side, that mean runs through the middle of the disc.

A generative policy learns the distribution of paths and samples from it. The toy integrates the exact flow-matching velocity for this two-way mixture of paths from fresh Gaussian noise, which stands in for a perfectly trained network, and every sample lands on one side. Diffusion Policy samples with a DDPM denoiser, which targets the same distribution. The paper's example is Push-T, where the end-effector can pass the T block on either side and Diffusion Policy commits to one side within each rollout (Sec. 4.1, Fig. 3).

The least-squares path runs 0.53 inside the disc at an even split, and none of the 200 generative samples touch it. Slide the share going left: the mean path moves aside only as one side comes to dominate, and it first clears the disc at 80 percent, while the samples follow the split.

Committing to a chunk keeps the policy on one side

Running several steps of each sampled chunk before replanning keeps consecutive actions on one mode, while sampling every step afresh lets the policy dither between the two.

Diffusion Policy predicts Tp actions from the latest To observations, runs the first Ta, and replans. The paper uses To = 2, Tp = 16, and Ta = 8 for Push-T (Tab. 7) and finds an action horizon of 8 best on most tasks, longer ones reacting too slowly (Sec. 5.3, Fig. 5). Drawing each action independently from a two-mode distribution lets consecutive actions come from different modes, which the paper argues gives jittery motion that alternates between them (Sec. 4.3).

The toy policy observes only its position, predicts 16 steps, and runs Ta of them. The sampling policy picks a side from its posterior given that position, read with a blur b, and draws a demonstration-like chunk on that side. The blur stands in for a learned policy that smooths over small offsets. The least-squares policy runs the conditional mean chunk.

Sampling a fresh side every step (Ta = 1) at b = 0.2 flips sides 5.14 times per rollout after the fork and hits the disc in 29 of 200 rollouts, while Ta = 8 flips 0.13 times and hits in 2. The least-squares policy hits in all 200 at Ta = 8. Set b to 0: a one-step sampler still flips 1.41 times but never hits, and the least-squares policy hits only when it runs long chunks, 51 of 200 at Ta = 8.

Flow and diffusion models in control

π0: A Vision-Language-Action Flow Model for General Robot Control

Black et al. · 2024 · RSS 2025

Attaches a flow-matching action expert of about 300M parameters to the 3B PaliGemma vision-language model. The expert turns Gaussian noise into a chunk of 50 future actions in ten Euler steps, conditioned on the backbone's view of the images, the instruction, and the robot's state.

Ten Euler steps turn noise into a 50-step chunk

The action expert starts from a chunk of pure Gaussian noise and follows a learned velocity for ten Euler steps of size 0.1, and on this toy the chunk usually commits to one way of moving within the first three.

π0 writes a chunk as A = (aₜ, …, aₜ₊₄₉), H = 50 future actions. Training mixes it with Gaussian noise ε into τA + (1 − τ)ε and regresses the expert's velocity onto A − ε. Sampling starts from pure noise at τ = 0 and takes ten forward-Euler steps of δ = 0.1, each adding δ times the predicted velocity (Sec. IV). Keys and values for the images, the instruction, and the state are cached, so each step reruns only the expert. The robot runs 16 or 25 of the 50 actions before the next chunk is drawn (App. A-D).

Training draws τ from a shifted Beta distribution, p(τ) = Beta((s − τ)/s; 1.5, 1) with s = 0.999, which favors the noisy end (App. A-B). The paper's reason: at high noise the expert must predict the mean action given the observation, which is hard because an observation constrains the action far more than a text label constrains an image. This schedule puts 41 percent of training draws below τ = 0.3, the stretch in which most of this toy's chunks commit to a mode.

The toy's actions are 2D, its chunk has π0's 50 steps, and its velocity is the exact one for a three-way mixture of demonstration chunks, standing in for a perfectly trained expert. A single Euler step lands every chunk on the average of the three ways, the least-squares answer, since the velocity at τ = 0 points from each noise sample to the mean.

The chunk plays from noise on arrival. Drag τ to stop at any of the ten jumps, and drag the scene sideways to turn it. Switch to one step: every chunk lands on the average of the three ways, a path no demonstration takes. Over 300 noises on this toy, ten steps give mode shares of 43, 43, and 14 percent against a target of 45, 35, and 20, and a mean distance of 0.21 from the exact flow's chunk, while 50 steps give 45, 33, and 21.

Learned sampling from unnormalized densities

Boltzmann generators: Sampling equilibrium states of many-body systems with deep learning

Noé et al. · 2019 · Science 365, eaaw1147; arXiv 1812.01729

Trains an invertible network to map a Gaussian onto a Boltzmann distribution, by energy and by example, and reweights its samples by exp(−u(x))/q(x) so that averages come out exact. It opened the question of how those weights behave as systems grow.

Reweighting corrects only where the flow has samples

A Boltzmann generator reweights each of its samples by the ratio of the Boltzmann density to its own, which makes the proportions exact wherever the network puts samples and blind wherever it puts none.

The paper's double well is E(x, y) = x⁴/4 − 3x² + x + y²/2 (Fig. 2 and its supplement), taken here along x, since y is an independent harmonic. The left well holds 99.2 percent of the Boltzmann mass at kT = 1 and the right one 0.8 percent, 4.78 kT higher in free energy. The network is a monotone map x = F(z) of a standard normal, a one-layer network of 13 tanh units, trained in the page with Adam.

Training by energy minimizes the average of u(F(z)) − log F′(z) over latent draws z, with u = E/kT, the paper's KL loss (Eq. 1). Training by example minimizes the negative log-likelihood of simulation data, here two short Metropolis runs held one in each well, as in the paper's Fig. 2a. The Both setting follows the paper's recipe for this system, a stage by example and then example and energy with equal weight. The weights w = exp(−u(x))/q(x) then turn the flow's samples into Boltzmann averages (Methods, Eq. 15).

The energy-trained flow falls into the deep well and stays there, the collapse to a single metastable state that the paper reports for energy training alone (Fig. S2). Its weights are nearly equal, so the effective sample size reads close to 100 percent while a whole well is missing. Adding the energy term to the example term barely moves mass across a high barrier: at kT = 1 the effective sample size stays near a third, and at kT = 2.5 it rises from 50.5 to 72.4 percent.

The example-trained flow holds 47 percent of its samples in the right well, so its own profile shows two level wells and a low barrier, yet the reweighted dots land on the exact profile: a right-well share of 0.81 percent against 0.83, and a gap of 4.80 kT against 4.78, at an effective sample size of 34 percent. Switch to Energy: the flow reports an effective sample size of 99.9 percent and puts no samples in the right well, so its reweighted share is 0. Raise kT to 2.5 and the energy-trained flow starts to find the right well.

Importance weights multiply across particles

The weight of a configuration of N independent particles is the product of N one-particle weights, so the effective sample size falls exponentially with N, and an estimate from samples cannot see a well the flow never visits.

The paper's systems are many-body, and its reweighting runs over every degree of freedom at once. The toy takes N copies of the double well at kT = 1 and moves each particle with the one-particle map from the figure above. The exact effective sample size of a configuration is then the one-particle value raised to the power N.

The flow trained by example covers both wells, and its estimate from 1,000 configurations follows the exact value for a few particles before it bottoms out near one effective sample. The flow trained by energy never samples the right well, so its weights look nearly equal and its estimate stays high, while its exact effective sample size is below 10⁻¹⁰⁰ from a single particle on. The configurations it misses, those with any particle in the right well, grow to most of the Boltzmann mass.

The energy-trained flow's estimate reads 94.9 percent at N = 64, while 41.5 percent of the Boltzmann mass has a particle in the well it never samples. One configuration carries 11 percent of the total weight at 256 particles, and the estimate drops to 7.22 percent. The example-trained flow's estimate falls from 36.9 percent at one particle to 2.18 percent at four, where the exact value is 1.25, and from eight particles on it sits near one sample in 1,000 while the exact value keeps falling.

Learned sampling from unnormalized densities

No Trick, No Treat: Pursuits and Challenges Towards Simulation-free Training of Neural Samplers

He et al. · 2025 · ICLR 2025 workshop on Frontiers in Probabilistic Inference

Finds that nearly all working diffusion and control-based neural samplers lean on Langevin preconditioning, the target's score built into the network, and that most fail to cover even a simple target without it. Parallel tempering followed by a fitted diffusion model reaches comparable samples with far fewer energy evaluations, and the authors propose that pair as the baseline to beat.

Hot copies cross the barriers and hand their states down

Parallel tempering runs copies of a sampler on a ladder of temperatures, where the hot copies cross energy barriers freely, and swaps states between neighbours so that the copy at T = 1 keeps receiving states from new modes.

The target is a 16-mode mixture in the plane, modes 0.5 wide and at least 4.5 apart, a smaller cousin of the paper's 40-mode benchmark. The climb from a mode to the midpoint toward its nearest neighbour costs 9.6 kT at T = 1, so a Langevin chain stays in the mode it first falls into.

Eight replicas sit at temperatures from 1 to 40 in geometric steps, and each plane shades its replica's tempered density, the target raised to the power 1/T, flat at the top and peaked at the bottom. Each replica takes one Metropolis-adjusted Langevin step per sweep, and neighbours propose to swap states, accepted with probability min(1, exp(Δ(1/T) · ΔE)), both differences taken between the same two replicas in the same order. Each Langevin step costs one evaluation of the energy and its gradient.

The step's drift is the target's score, the term that working neural samplers carry inside their networks. The paper reads that term as running MCMC inside the sampler, which blurs the line between data-free and data-driven methods (Sec. 5).

Watch the hot replicas wander while the T = 1 replica jumps between modes each time a swap hands it a new state, and drag sideways to turn the stack. The T = 1 replica of the first run visits 14 of the 16 modes within 1,000 energy evaluations and all 16 by about 2,500, while eight plain Langevin chains on the same budget stay in the 7 modes they started near. About 79 percent of swaps are accepted.

On the same budget, tempering finds every mode and plain Langevin keeps its first ones

Parallel tempering's single T = 1 chain ends up on every mode in proportion, while the same budget of energy evaluations spent on eight plain Langevin chains leaves most modes unvisited.

The paper's argument is about cost. Its Fig. 2 plots sample quality against target evaluations on the 40-mode mixture, with parallel tempering followed by a fitted diffusion model as one of the curves, and the authors conclude that almost all neural samplers "require several orders of magnitude more target evaluations compared to PT" (Sec. 4).

Its Table 4 isolates the ingredient that makes neural samplers work. DDS trained with reverse KL on that target reaches an MMD of 0.074 with Langevin preconditioning and 1.497 without it, and CMCD 0.075 against 4.011, lower being better. Most objectives collapse without the term, even from a starting point that covers every mode (Sec. 4).

Both methods start from the same eight points and spend eight energy evaluations per sweep. Parallel tempering keeps only its T = 1 chain, one sample per sweep, and plain Langevin keeps all eight of its chains. The chart averages four runs.

Slide the budget. Plain Langevin starts ahead because its eight chains begin in about six modes at once, but they never leave them, and 0.635 of its samples sit on the wrong modes at every budget. Tempering passes it at 256 evaluations, has found all 16 modes in all four runs by 3,984, and is down to 0.034 at 158,496.

Molecules, proteins, and materials

Proteina: Scaling Flow-based Protein Structure Generative Models

Geffner et al. · 2025 · ICLR 2025, oral

Runs plain flow matching on Cα coordinates with a non-equivariant transformer, up to about 21 million AlphaFold structures, and fold-class labels for control, and generates designable backbones up to 800 residues. Its headline designability comes from a sampler with reduced noise, the choice the second figure computes.

Flow matching on 180 Cα coordinates

Proteína treats a 60-residue backbone as the 180 coordinates of its Cα atoms and moves Gaussian noise onto a fold with the same averaged velocity as the first-principles figures, committing to a fold long before the chain looks like one.

Proteína drops the residue frames of earlier backbone models and keeps only Cα positions, in nanometres. Noise and data are both centered, the prior is a standard Gaussian, and the path is the straight line x_t = t x₁ + (1 − t) x₀ (Sections 3.2 and I.1, and the released code). In those units a 60-residue noise cloud has a radius of gyration of 1.72 nm, close to the 1.20 to 1.57 nm of the folds here.

The data on this page are four 60-residue folds built from textbook geometry: an α hairpin, a three-helix bundle, a β-meander, and a βαβ unit, weighted toward the α folds as Proteína's own samples are. For that data the averaged velocity has a closed form, integrated here with RK4 in 200 steps on Proteína's log-spaced time grid. A fold-class label restricts the average to one class, and guidance mixes labelled and unlabelled velocities, v = ω v(x, c) + (1 − ω) v(x, ∅), as the paper's Eq. 4 does. On this toy each fold sits at one orientation, while Proteína trains on every rotation of each structure (Section 3.3), which the closed form leaves out.

Training draws t from 0.02 U(0, 1) + 0.98 Beta(1.9, 1), which puts most of the regression near the data end: only 27% of training examples have t below 0.5 (Section 3.2, Appendix K). One readout gives that share for the current t.

Press Play to watch fresh noise draws. The bars settle on one fold around t = 0.19 in the median draw, while the chain still looks like noise, and the chain is tightest near t = 0.6, where two independent clouds average to a smaller one. The landing readout puts the unlabelled flow on the four folds in roughly the proportions of their weights, 35, 30, 15, and 20%, give or take the few points of noise in 300 draws. Pick Mainly β and every draw becomes the β-meander. Pick Mainly α and raise ω to 3: the α hairpin's share of α samples rises from about half to about two thirds, because guidance pushes away from what the unlabelled model expects.

Lowering γ sharpens samples without tempering them

Proteína's stochastic sampler with noise scale γ = 1 targets the same distribution as the ODE, and the γ below 1 behind its headline designability narrows every mode and reweights them in a way true tempering would not.

The sampler adds a Langevin term to the flow, dx = [v + g(t) s] dt + √(2 g(t) γ) dW, with the score read off the velocity, s = (t v − x)/(1 − t) (Eqs. 2 and 3). With γ = 1 any choice of g(t) leaves the marginals unchanged. The paper uses g(t) = 1/(t + 0.01), 400 log-spaced steps, and plain ODE steps after t = 0.99 (Appendix I.4), and the figure runs exactly that on the three-bump mixture of the first-principles section, where v is exact.

Proteína's authors call reducing γ "not a principled way to reduce the temperature" and keep it because it improves designability at the cost of diversity (Section 3.4). For the 200M model its Table 3 reports 19.6% designability with the ODE, and its Table 1 reports 91.4%, 96.4%, and 98.2% at γ = 0.5, 0.45, and 0.35, with 323, 305, and 239 designable clusters against 91 for the ODE.

Start at γ = 1: the histogram sits on the data, as the ODE's does. Slide γ down. Every mode narrows, and the mode at 0.4 grows at the expense of the one at 2.2: at γ = 0.45 the shares are 45, 42, and 13% against the data's 45, 35, and 20%, while true tempering would have grown the mode at −1.8, the largest. At γ = 0 every sample ends in the mode at 0.4, the one nearest the single early bump the paths collapse onto while the score term acts hardest, and tempering's limit would instead put everything on the highest peak, at −1.8.

Molecules, proteins, and materials

Rethinking Self-Consistency in Protein Generative Models

Lee et al. · 2026 · ICML 2026 workshop on Generative and Agentic AI for Biology, poster

Shows that self-consistency, the refold-and-compare test behind every designability number, rejects 44% of native sequence-structure pairs, finds the failures concentrated among flexible proteins, and proposes checking against a predicted conformational ensemble instead of a single refold. Its full text was not publicly readable when this page was built, so the figures compute the check on a toy and quote only the abstract.

One refold rejects a flexible native

Self-consistency compares a structure with one refold, so a protein that genuinely moves fails whenever its deposited snapshot sits away from the folder's single answer.

The check folds the sequence, superposes the prediction on the structure, and accepts if the RMSD falls under a threshold, 2 Å in Proteína's designability (Appendix F). Self-consistency rejects 44% of native sequence-structure pairs, the paper finds. It splits the failures into flexibility failures, where one refold cannot stand for a broad ensemble, and folder failures, and finds both more common among flexible proteins in ATLAS molecular-dynamics trajectories.

The toy is a two-helix protein whose second helix swings on its loop with spread τ. The native is one snapshot of that ensemble. The folder is ideal and returns the most populated conformation with 0.3 Å of coordinate error. Ensemble self-consistency, the paper's proposal, compares against predicted conformations instead; here the ensemble is eight draws from the true ensemble and the check takes the closest, a rule chosen for this page because the abstract does not state the paper's.

The first snapshot swings 14°: the one refold sits 2.40 Å away and fails, while the closest of the eight ensemble members sits 1.39 Å away and passes. Press New snapshot a few times. A snapshot that swings more than about 13° fails the single refold, since a 15° swing alone costs 2.4 Å. Set τ to 0 and every snapshot passes, with about 0.6 Å of jitter left over.

Recall against flexibility, one refold and an ensemble

Run the check on many snapshots: the share of natives one refold accepts falls as the protein gets more flexible, while an ensemble keeps recall high and still rejects decoys.

Each point is 240 natives at one flexibility, each checked against a single refold and against an ensemble, plus 240 decoys: the same chain with its second helix turned on its own axis by 90 to 270°, a packing error that no swing reproduces. Ensemble self-consistency, in the paper's tests, improves native recall across the flexibility spectrum, rescues co-design generations that the single-refold check rejected, and keeps its specificity on a Rosetta decoy set.

Specificity holds on this toy because the decoys sit 2.1 to 3.1 Å from the native, and no swing brings one below 2 Å. A looser threshold lets the ensemble accept them.

At 2 Å and τ = 12° one refold accepts 72% of natives and an ensemble of 8 accepts 94%, and neither accepts a decoy. Raise the threshold to 3 Å: recall reaches 88 and 99%, and decoys start to pass, 33% against one refold and 59% against the ensemble. Set the ensemble size to 1 and the dashed native curve falls below the solid one, 53% against 72%, since one random conformation is a worse guess than the most populated one.

Transport between datasets and scientific inference

InverseBench: Benchmarking Plug-and-Play Diffusion Priors for Inverse Problems in Physical Sciences

Zheng et al. · 2025 · ICLR 2025, spotlight

Benchmarks 14 plug-and-play diffusion-prior methods against domain baselines on five inverse problems from optical tomography, MRI, black-hole imaging, seismology, and fluid dynamics. With a suitable prior they generally beat conventional baselines, sometimes lose to well-initialized solvers, cost more compute, and barely move when the forward operator changes.

DPS against the exact posterior

DPS steers a diffusion prior with the likelihood of its denoised guess and ignores how unsure that guess is, so at low noise it overfits the measurement and sends samples where the prior has no mass.

Guidance methods add ∇ log p_t(y | x_t) to the prior's flow, and that term is intractable. DPS replaces it with the likelihood at the denoised guess x̂ = E[x₁ | x_t] (DPS, Eq. 16). The exact term averages the likelihood over everything x₁ could still be, and the difference is the spread of x₁ given x_t, which DPS drops.

On this toy everything is exact: the five-cluster prior of the first-principles section, a measurement of the first coordinate with noise σ, and a posterior that is again a Gaussian mixture, sampled in closed form. DPS runs on the same prior flow with guidance weight ζ/σ², where ζ = 1 is the Gaussian weight of its derivation. The published DPS normalizes each step by the residual instead, and its own ablation found the 1/σ² weight gave poor images (Appendix C.3).

InverseBench scores reconstructions by PSNR, SSIM, and data misfit, covers only problems whose ground truth is unimodal, and lists multimodal posteriors as an open benchmark (Appendix C). It also finds that methods querying the forward model many times tend to beat simpler ones like DPS, at the cost of more tuning and compute.

With x₁ = 0 and σ = 0.1 the exact posterior sits on cluster 2 alone, while about half of DPS's samples end in empty space, mostly below, near no cluster. No guidance scale on the slider repairs it: from ζ = 0.1 to 3, between 46 and 54% of DPS samples stay off the prior. Slide σ up and the side curve falls to near zero by σ = 2, where a weak measurement leaves both near the prior. At x₁ = 2.2 the gap is worst at the lowest noise, with 98% of DPS samples off the prior at σ = 0.05.

Turning the operator: supervised against plug-and-play

A supervised network bakes its training operator into its weights, while a plug-and-play method reads the operator at inference time, and InverseBench measured the consequence: a changed MRI mask moved end-to-end methods by 9.58 dB and diffusion priors by 0.48 dB.

The controlled experiment keeps compressed-sensing MRI at the same sparsity and turns the subsampling lines from vertical to horizontal. The average absolute change was 0.48 dB of PSNR for plug-and-play diffusion methods, 1.62 dB for traditional baselines, and 9.58 dB for end-to-end methods, for which the new mask is out of distribution (Section 4.3).

The toy keeps the turn and nothing else. The prior is twelve clusters on a ring, so a turned measurement is exactly as hard as the original, and each estimate gets one projection with noise 0.1. The supervised estimator is the best possible one for the training direction: the posterior mean of x given y under a(0), which least squares on paired data converges to. The plug-and-play estimate computes the posterior mean under the turned direction, from the same prior.

At 90° the supervised estimator loses 4.65 dB of PSNR and the plug-and-play estimate gains 0.18 dB, both over 1,500 test pairs. Both err, since one projection of a ring cannot say which side a point sits on, but the supervised estimates land along the training direction, far from where the turned measurement points. Turn back toward 0° and the two estimators converge, since at 0° they are the same function.

Transport between datasets and scientific inference

A Trust Crisis In Simulation-Based Inference? Your Posterior Approximations Can Be Unfaithful

Hermans et al. · 2021 · TMLR, November 2022

Measures the expected coverage of posterior approximations from neural posterior estimation, neural ratio estimation, sequential neural likelihood, and ABC on seven benchmarks, finds that every method can be overconfident, and shows that ensembles of posterior estimators cover more.

Coverage separates overconfident from conservative

Check a posterior approximation by simulating pairs (θ∗, x) and counting how often its 1 − α credible region holds θ∗: a calibrated approximation lands on the diagonal, and an overconfident one falls below it.

The expected coverage of the 1 − α highest-density regions is the probability, over the simulator's joint distribution, that the region computed from x contains the θ∗ that produced x (Definition 2.1), estimated by averaging over simulated pairs (Eq. 5). Curves above the diagonal are conservative and curves below it are overconfident, and the paper argues that science should prefer the first.

On this toy simulator, θ ~ N(0, 1) and x | θ ~ N(θ, 0.6²), the posterior is known, so the approximation can be made too narrow, too wide, or biased on purpose. A divergence cannot tell the two failures apart. The best classifier separating approximation from posterior has an AUROC of 0.71 at both half and twice the true width, about the 0.7 that the paper's Figure 1 shows for an overconfident and a conservative approximation alike.

Coverage is not the whole test either. The prior itself is perfectly calibrated and uninformative, as the paper notes after Definition 2.2, and the log-density gain readout shows the difference.

At half the true width the 90% region holds θ∗ only about 59% of the time, the dots fall below the diagonal, and the log-density gain is −0.11 nats, worse than using the prior. Slide to twice the width and coverage climbs to nearly 100% while the AUROC stays the same. A bias of one posterior sd drops the 90% region to 74% even at the right width. Switch to the prior: coverage sits on the diagonal and the gain is zero.

Averaging overconfident estimators raises coverage

Each member of an ensemble errs in its own direction, so their average is wider than any one of them and covers the truth more often, though not always as often as it claims.

Ensembles in the paper average the approximate posteriors of five independently trained estimators. In its Figure 3 deep ensembles consistently have a higher expected coverage than the average single model, and Appendix E shows coverage rising with ensemble size (Observation 3). The ensemble can still be non-conservative, and bagging does not always help.

On the toy each member is too narrow by the width factor, and its mean is off by an independent error of τ posterior sds, the way separately trained networks disagree. The average of the members' densities carries that disagreement as extra width. The ensemble's credible regions are found on a grid, as in the paper's Appendix A.

With members at 0.7 of the true width and errors of 0.5 sd, one member's 90% region holds θ∗ 70% of the time and an ensemble of five holds it 82% of the time: higher, and still short of 90%. Set the ensemble size to 1 and coverage falls back to a single member's. Set τ to 0 and the members agree, so averaging adds nothing.

Media generation and serving

Scaling Rectified Flow Transformers for High-Resolution Image Synthesis

Patrick Esser et al. · 2024 · ICML 2024

Stability AI trained 61 formulations of the diffusion objective at fixed architecture and data, found that rectified flow with logit-normal timestep sampling ranked best, added a resolution-dependent shift of the timestep schedule, and scaled an MMDiT to 8B parameters. Later media generators share its flow-matching objective, and Wan's video models its logit-normal sampling too.

The regression is hardest in the middle of the path

At both ends of the path the best prediction of the velocity target is a straight line in z, and only in between does the network have to learn the shape of the data.

SD3 writes the path as zₜ = (1 − t)x₀ + tε, with data x₀ at t = 0 and noise ε at t = 1, the reverse of the figures above, and trains the network to predict ε − x₀ from zₜ. Section 3.1 argues this target is hardest in the middle. At t = 0 the input is the data point itself, so the best prediction is the noise mean minus z. At t = 1 the input is the noise, so it is z minus the data mean.

On the page's three-cluster mixture the best prediction E[ε − x₀ | zₜ] and its spread have closed forms, and the figure integrates them over z at each t. The part of the best prediction that no straight line in z fits is zero at both ends, peaks near t = 0.34, and has about 82% of its total between t = 0.25 and 0.75. The loss the best predictor still pays rises from 1 at the data end to 3.62 near t = 0.74 and ends at 2.64, the data's variance, at the noise end.

Drag t or press Play. At t = 0 the pairs form one straight band and at t = 1 three parallel bands, one per cluster, and in both cases the best prediction is a straight line. In between, the best prediction bends around the clusters and the dashed line misses it.

Logit-normal sampling spends training on the middle

Drawing u from N(m, s) and passing it through the logistic function trains the middle of the path more often than uniform sampling, and among the variants SD3 compared it ranked first.

Changing the density of training times from uniform to π(t) is the same as weighting the rectified-flow loss by π(t) (Equation 18), so the sampler decides where on the path the network's capacity goes. SD3 compares the logit-normal density, a mode density with heavier tails that stays positive at both endpoints, and CosMap, the cosine schedule's log signal-to-noise ratio mapped onto the straight path. The figure keeps SD3's time, data at 0 and noise at 1, so positive m means more noise.

Table 1 ranks the variants by non-dominated sorting on CLIP score and FID over 24 combinations of sampler setting, EMA weights, and dataset. rf/lognorm(0.00, 1.00) has the best average rank, 1.54, and uniform rectified flow ranks 5.67. rf/lognorm(0.50, 0.60) ranks first with 50 sampling steps and 8.50 with 5.

Pick a variant or move m and s. The histogram of 3,000 draws, made the way the paper makes them, matches each density. lognorm(0.5, 0.6) puts 84% of training times in the middle half against 50% for uniform, and ranks first at 50 sampling steps and worst of these six at 5.

More pixels see through the same noise

At the same t, an image with α² times the pixels gives away its content α times more precisely, so SD3 shifts high-resolution training and sampling toward noise with t → αt / (1 + (α − 1)t).

Section 5.3.2 derives the shift from a constant image. Each pixel of z = (1 − t)c + tε is one noisy look at c, so the mean of n pixels divided by 1 − t estimates c with standard deviation t / ((1 − t)√n). An image with α² times the pixels reaches the same uncertainty at tₘ = αt / (1 + (α − 1)t), which lowers the log signal-to-noise ratio by 2 log α at every t.

The paper calls constant images unrealistic and picks α by a human preference study on a model trained at 1024 × 1024. Raters strongly preferred shifts above 1.5, and SD3 uses α = 3.0 for training and sampling at that resolution. Self Forcing inherits the same map from Wan2.1 with a factor of 5.

At t = 0.5 and α = 3 the small image's estimate has standard deviation 0.063 and the large image's 0.021. Switch the large image to the shifted time, tₘ = 0.75: it looks noisier pixel by pixel, and its estimate is now exactly as uncertain as the small image's.

Media generation and serving

Self Forcing: Bridging the Train-Test Gap in Autoregressive Video Diffusion

Xun Huang et al. · 2025 · NeurIPS 2025 spotlight

Self Forcing trains a causal, few-step video model on its own autoregressive rollouts and scores each whole generated video with a distribution-matching loss, so the model learns from the contexts it will see at inference. Its DMD and SiD versions use no video data, and the chunk-wise model streams at 17 frames per second on one H100.

A model never shown its own errors carries them forward

Teacher forcing trains each frame on real previous frames, so its loss cannot see how the model treats artifacts it makes itself, and training on the model's own rollouts is what lets the loss see them.

Self Forcing rolls the causal student out during training the way it runs at inference: each frame is denoised in 4 steps, conditioned through the KV cache on frames the student made itself, and the whole video is scored by a distribution-matching loss. The DMD version compares noised rollouts against a pretrained Wan2.1-T2V-14B and uses no videos. Gradients flow through one denoising step per frame and stop at the KV cache of earlier frames. Teacher forcing and diffusion forcing condition on frames of training videos instead, clean or noised.

In the toy, each frame has content, which real frames vary in, and an artifact channel that real frames never use. The generator adds an artifact of size 0.1 to every frame it makes and carries a fraction k of its context's artifact into the next frame. Real contexts carry no artifact, so the teacher-forced loss is the same for every k, and a model that copies its last frame forward stays at k = 1. On its own rollouts the context carries the artifact, and the loss pulls k to 0.

At k = 1 the artifact's standard deviation grows as 0.1 times the square root of the frame index and reaches 0.77 at frame 60. The paper reports the video version: its baselines degrade more as the number of autoregressive steps grows, usually as progressive over-saturation or over-sharpening, and in the frame-wise ablation Self Forcing with DMD scores 84.26 on VBench against 78.12 for teacher forcing with DMD.

Press Train on own rollouts. The teacher-forced loss stays at 3.90e-4 whatever k is, while the rollout loss falls from 0.24 to 3.9e-4 as k goes from 1 to 0 in about 225 steps, and the artifact at frame 60 drops from 0.77 to 0.10. Drag k above 1: the teacher-forced strip blows up, and its loss on real contexts does not move.

How the field got here

2,501 words.

The core idea and the field's edges

Stefano Peluchetti argued in a paper submitted to ICLR 2022 that "the time-reversal argument, common to all denoising diffusion probabilistic modeling proposals, is not necessary." His replacement pins a simple random process to a data point, the conditioning Joseph Doob formalized in 1957, and swaps the mixture of pinned processes for one Markov process with the same marginals, whose drift, by a 1986 theorem of István Gyöngy, is their conditional average. Conditional averages are least-squares targets, so a network learns that drift by regression on pinned paths without simulating the process. The 2023 DSBM paper noted that "the concept of Markovian projection has been rediscovered multiple times," and option pricing uses it for local volatility. Three groups published the noiseless version within a month in 2022, and Meta's name for it, flow matching, stuck.

The field is the set of people who asked what else pinning and averaging can carry. One question divides it by what gets regressed: a velocity in flow matching, its integral in flow maps, which sample in one step, or jump rates over tokens in discrete and edit flows. Another divides it by what sits at the ends. Noise and data give generation, data and data give Schrödinger bridges, and an energy or a reward in place of data gives Boltzmann sampling and tilting toward p_base(x)·exp(r(x)/β). With samples at only one end, the correction to learn is the gradient of a value function, and the field returns to stochastic optimal control, whose central trick Bert Kappen traced in 2005: "The log transform goes back to Schrödinger and was first used in control theory by" Wendell Fleming in 1977.

The community's events draw the same boundary. Its August 2026 workshop at Microsoft Research New England treated generative modeling, sampling, and stochastic control as one subject. Diffusion language models are splitting off, with a NeurIPS 2026 workshop and serving problems of their own. Outside sit the methods that keep deciding the field's contests, among them autoregression, proper scoring rules, parallel tempering, retrieval, and plain regression.

Older lines, 1931 to 2020

In 1931, in a paper on the reversal of the laws of nature, Schrödinger posed the bridge problem by asking for the most likely evolution of a diffusing gas observed at two times in an unlikely arrangement. He extended it in 1932, and his 2021 translators credit the 1931 paper with shaping Bernstein's reciprocal processes and Kolmogorov's 1937 work on reversibility. Hans Föllmer recast the problem in 1988 as entropy minimization over path measures, and Paolo Dai Pra showed in 1991 that it is a stochastic control problem.

The reversal inside diffusion models has a physics ancestor. Edward Nelson's 1966 stochastic mechanics split a diffusion's drift into a current velocity, which carries the density without noise, and an osmotic velocity proportional to the gradient of the log density, and in a 1998 restatement the forward and backward drifts differ by twice the osmotic term. By this essay's own reading, the osmotic velocity is the score times the diffusion coefficient, and the current velocity drives the probability-flow ODE. The 2020 score-SDE paper credits the reversal to Anderson's 1982 theorem and does not cite Nelson.

Control supplied the tilt. Fleming's logarithmic transformation linearized a class of nonlinear control problems, Kappen built path-integral control on it, and Todorov linearized another class in 2009 by charging control for its divergence from passive dynamics. Relative entropy policy search gave RL the same exponential reweighting in 2010, and Korbak, Perez, and Buckley argued in 2022 that fine-tuning a language model is "best viewed as Bayesian inference" toward a tilted target.
