Learned sampling from unnormalized densities

A Boltzmann generator for mW ice in one PyTorch file

nano, end to end

Write a Boltzmann generator for mW ice in one PyTorch file, match the published sampling efficiency at 64 and 216 molecules, and measure how fast it collapses as the crystal grows to 1,728.

Effective sample size against crystal size at a fixed per-molecule error

When every molecule adds the same small KL, log-weights add up over molecules, so the effective sample size falls exponentially with N while the log-weight variance per molecule stays put.

Fitted to the paper's 64.7% at 64 molecules, the toy model is 3.2% too narrow, 0.0031 nats per molecule. Held there, the exact ESS falls to 23% at 216, 3.1% at 512 and 0.11% at 1,000, while the paper's model falls faster, to 16.4%, 0.6% and 0.04%. From 50,000 draws the toy's ESS reads 1.1% at 1,000, ten times the truth, because the largest weights go unsampled. The log-weight variance per molecule reads 0.006 at every size, the stable number the project plots.

Molecules, proteins, and materials

RetFold and the Domain Retrieval Rate, reimplemented

reimplement a paper

Rebuild RetFold, the CPU baseline that glues real CATH domains together, and measure how much of what Proteina, FrameFlow and BoltzGen produce is reassembled known structure.

Domain retrieval rate on toy backbones, under two ways to cut domains

A backbone counts as retrieved when any one of its domains aligns to a library domain above the alnTM bar, so the rate depends on the generator, on the bar, and on how the backbone is cut into domains.

At the 0.7 bar the RetFold recipe retrieves 100% and the novel generator 0%, the paper's ordering. At 0.5 the novel generator jumps to 75%, because its half-domains share helices with the library, and cutting coarser drops it to 55%. In the paper's Table 11, switching from Merizo to Chainsaw moves Chroma by −30.8 points at 0.7 and RetFold by +4.0, so the project pins segmentation before comparing with 95.8% for RetFold and 43.0% for FrameFlow.

Transport between datasets and scientific inference

Scoring a Schrödinger bridge against LARRY's lineage barcodes

apply something that exists

Run moscot, OT-CFM, and a Schrödinger bridge on the LARRY mouse blood time course, and score each one's neutrophil-versus-monocyte calls for day-2 cells against what their barcoded clones became.

Growth matters most when the coupling is sharp

An entropic coupling's fate calls for day-2 cells correlate with what each barcoded clone became, and on this toy leaving out growth costs most of that correlation when the coupling is close to plain optimal transport.

At a bridge noise of ε = 0.03 the balanced coupling must spend every progenitor's equal share on a snapshot that is 78 percent neutrophils, so monocyte-biased cells get pushed onto neutrophils, and r falls to 0.33 against 0.51 with growth. Warmer couplings blur that error and the curves meet near ε = 3, before the noise of 200 sampled endpoints per cell, scored as PRESCIENT scores them, pulls both down. New toy draws another population, and growth beat balanced at the smallest ε in 15 of 16 draws tested.

The scoreboard has no flow or bridge row

PRESCIENT's notebook scores four methods and a clonal ceiling on the same 335 day-2 cells, and the project fills the empty rows, starting with balanced moscot within 0.05 of Waddington-OT's r.

PRESCIENT falls from 0.407 to 0.035 when its growth term is removed, the largest effect on the board. Under AUROC the published methods sit between 0.52 and 0.73 against 0.77 for the clonal ceiling. The project's first check is balanced moscot inside the band, which says the protocol was rebuilt right before any bridge is scored.

Media generation and serving

LoL's RoPE jitter, rebuilt on LongLive

reimplement a paper

LongLive, NVIDIA's open real-time video model, starts snapping back to its opening frames about 33 seconds in, so rebuild LoL, the training-free fix whose authors released no code, and measure on 128 MovieGen prompts whether it stops the snapping without freezing the motion.

All twelve heads realign with the sink at once

LoL's phase coherence kernel, computed for Wan 2.1's 22 temporal RoPE frequencies, peaks within a frame of both collapses LoL reports, and jittering each head's base spreads those peaks so the heads stop peaking together.

With the head jitter at 0 every head shares one kernel, and up to frame 400 it reaches the frame-132 level only around frames 132, 163, and 201, two of which LoL reports as collapses. Raise the jitter to LoL's σ of 0.8 and the most heads at that level at once, anywhere from frame 132 to 400, averages 5.1 of 12 over 200 draws, while the mean coherence at frame 133 falls from 0.557 to 0.432. Slide the frame across 132 and the plain arrow lengthens as more of the 22 dots line up. The kernel ignores what each head attends to, so the project's sink-collapse score on generated video stays the test.

Only the jitter keeps motion without collapse

LoL's Table 1 puts each position method on two axes, and the reproduction is done when the plain row lands within 5 points of 30.54 and the jittered row at 6 or below with its motion within 2 points of the plain row.

On LongLive, position interpolation and YaRN stop the collapse by freezing the motion, at dynamic degree 0.35 and 2.67, while RIFLEx and plain extrapolation keep both the motion and the collapse. Only LoL's row sits low on collapse and level with plain extrapolation on motion. Self-Forcing++ shows the same pattern at higher motion. The targets are drawn for LongLive's average score, which the project's done-when names.

A semester

Reward tilting

Which KL keeps SD3.5-M's pictures intact when the reward is OCR

apply something that exists

Fine-tune Stable Diffusion 3.5 Medium to render text six ways that differ only in how they hold it near the original model, and use a separate vision-language judge to see which keeps the rest of the picture intact as the OCR score climbs.

Which steps each penalty guards, and what that does to the picture

Flow-GRPO’s shipped KL weighs the last steps before the data almost exclusively, and on a toy picture whose text and rest move together, how a penalty weighs the steps decides how much of the rest survives at a given OCR score.

The shipped KL puts 76% of its weight on the last trained step and 97% on the last three, the paper’s form 64% and 92%, and the velocity gap a flat 11% per step. With coupling 0.8 and no blind spot, gold at OCR 0.90 is 1.000 for RAM, 0.994 for the shipped KL, 0.982 at noise 1.414, and 0.755 for the velocity gap, the curve no KL also follows on this toy. At coupling 0 every arm keeps the picture. At coupling 0.6 with a blind spot of 0.3 the order flips, 0.992 for the velocity gap against 0.977 for RAM, because the exact tilt follows the reward wherever it points.

Flow maps and one-step generation

Six flow-map objectives in one PyTorch file, then the price of the JVP

nano, end to end

Write Boffi's three self-distillation losses, MeanFlow, and SplitMeanFlow in one PyTorch file, match Boffi's 3.34 CIFAR-10 FID at four steps, then measure what the derivative-based losses cost in GPU-hours against the derivative-free ones.

The boxes LSD has to land in, and what each loss costs

The file is done when its LSD lands in two boxes around Boffi’s CIFAR-10 numbers, and in network evaluations per example the JVP losses cost a little less than the three-pass ones, so their price has to show up elsewhere.

LSD has to land within 0.8 of 8.10 at one step and within 0.35 of 3.34 at four. At the project’s diagonal share of 0.75 and the paper’s C of about 1.5, a training example costs 1.38 network evaluations for LSD, ESD, or MeanFlow and 1.50 for PSD or SplitMeanFlow, a ratio of 0.92. With no diagonal share the costs are 2.5 and 3. ESD has no image rows because it diverged.

In PyTorch the JVP’s price is attention memory

Forward-mode differentiation pushes the JVP losses onto PyTorch’s math attention, which keeps a tokens-by-tokens tensor per head and layer for the backward pass, a cost that grows with the square of the image’s token count.

At the project’s 256 tokens and a batch of 128 in fp32, math attention keeps 2.42 GB of probabilities, 18.9 MB per image, and attention is 10% of the FLOPs, so even a kernel twice as slow adds at most a tenth to a forward pass. At 1,024 tokens the same batch keeps 38.65 GB and attention is 31% of the FLOPs. A model that counts one probability tensor per head and layer and nothing else.

Discrete, edit, and diffusion language models

The data-constrained crossover, rebuilt and tested against a regularized AR

reimplement a paper

Rebuild in plain PyTorch the NeurIPS 2025 experiment where masked diffusion beat GPT-style models on 100 million C4 tokens repeated hundreds of times, then see whether the GPT-style model catches up once it gets the dropout and weight decay a later paper credits.

What repeated data is worth to each objective

Prabhudesai et al. fit how fast repeated epochs lose value, a half-life of 31.93 epochs for AR against 512.85 for masked diffusion, and the project asks whether dropout and weight decay can move AR’s number.

At 256 epochs AR’s data is worth 32.9 times its unique tokens and diffusion’s 201.9 times, and a regularizer that lifted AR’s half-life to 100 would reach 93.2. The frontier puts the crossover at 2.3 × 10¹⁸ FLOPs for 25M unique tokens, which the project’s largest 25M run passes, and at 4.7 × 10¹⁹ for 100M, which the 425M-parameter diffusion run at 500 epochs passes and the 140M AR run at 50 epochs does not. Those two runs are done when their best losses land within 0.03 of 3.55 and 3.71.

Flow and diffusion models in control

comma's world-model driving recipe, rebuilt in MetaDrive

reimplement a paper

Rebuild comma.ai's openpilot recipe, a driving policy that learns only inside a video world model, at small scale in the MetaDrive simulator, where each claim can be checked by driving, and measure how much of a commanded half-meter swerve the world model draws.

Lane-centre passes against what the world model executes

A policy trained inside a world model learns to recover only from the drift the model actually draws, so its pass rate on the lane-centre tests rises with the fraction of each commanded move the model executes.

Cloned from logs that never drift past 0.1 m, arm A passes 7 of 24. Trained inside a world model that draws 70% of each move, arm B passes 22, it passes all 24 from 85% up, and at 0% it passes 7, like the clone. comma's Table 2 has off-policy imitation at 5 of 24 and its world-model policy at 24. The paper shows its world model drawing a commanded 0.5 m swerve only in part, with no number, and that fraction is what the project measures.

Learned sampling from unnormalized densities

Gen-COMPAS from the paper alone, with a replica-exchange arm

reimplement a paper

Rebuild Gen-COMPAS, the 2026 Nature method that maps Trp-cage folding with 594 ns of simulation against D. E. Shaw's 208 µs, from the paper alone, and run replica exchange on the same budget beside it.

The loop's folding paths, and replica exchange at the same budget

Gen-COMPAS shoots short unbiased trajectories from generated points its committor puts near one half, so it collects folding paths at budgets where brute-force MD sees none, and the project adds the replica-exchange arm the paper lacks.

Slide through the rounds. After ten, near 70,000 MD steps, the loop has collected 9 to 31 folding paths across five test seeds, while a million steps of brute-force MD never leave the unfolded basin. Replica exchange with six replicas reaches the band between 10⁵ and 10⁶ steps. With 3,000 solvent degrees of freedom it needs 18 or 19 replicas and is still outside the band there. The free energy from the loop's paths is the project's measurement and is not computed here. Gen-COMPAS reports Trp-cage from 594 ns against D. E. Shaw's 208 µs.

Molecules, proteins, and materials

Crystal flow matching in one file, then delete the prototypes

nano, end to end

Write crystal flow matching as one readable training file, check it against FlowMM on MP-20, then retrain with whole families of known crystal prototypes deleted and see how much of the stability score was coming from them.

One training pair of crystal flow matching, on the torus, the lattice and the types

The one-file model regresses on straight paths in three spaces at once: fractional coordinates take the shortest way around the periodic cell, the lattice moves in log lengths and angles, and each atom's type stays masked until its own time.

Press Play, then switch the path to straight in the box. Over 200 noise draws torus paths average 0.47 to 0.48 of the cell against 0.59 to 0.74 for straight ones, and about half the atoms cross a face. The finished file must match FlowMM's 61.39% match rate on MP-20, and the holdout then deletes whole prototype families, which cost a structure-prediction model 50 to 78% of its accuracy.

Transport between datasets and scientific inference

GW150914 from strain to posterior in one file

nano, end to end

Write a flow-matching network in one file that turns LIGO's public GW150914 strain into the merger's 15 source parameters, then reweight its samples with the exact likelihood and check them against bilby's own GW150914 example.

Importance sampling turns a network's error into lost efficiency

Reweighting a network's samples by the exact likelihood corrects a moderate error and charges for it in sample efficiency, while a proposal that is too narrow or too far off still fails the 2 × 10⁻³ nat check at 20,000 samples.

At the default the proposal sits half a standard deviation off and 1.5 times too wide: 58.6 percent of its samples count, and reweighting takes the largest marginal JSD from 51 to 0.15 thousandths of a nat. At offset 2 the efficiency falls to 5.6 percent and reweighting gets the JSD only down to 3.0 thousandths, over the threshold, and a too-narrow proposal at width 0.7 fails at 4.5. At offset 0 and width 1, dropping the correlation leaves both marginals matching the posterior before reweighting, at 0.22 thousandths, while the efficiency halves to 48.7 percent. DINGO-IS reached 28.8 percent on GW150914, with its largest JSD at 1.4 thousandths. The toy chirp is a leading-order inspiral in two parameters.

Media generation and serving

CosyVoice from public audio on one GPU

nano, end to end

Train CosyVoice's two halves from public audio on one GPU, a small language model that writes speech tokens and a flow-matching model that turns them into spectrograms, and check them against the word error rate CosyVoice's paper reports for the same 585 hours of LibriTTS.

Guidance makes the decoder's frames more typical than recordings

CosyVoice's guidance of 0.7 pushes each generated frame toward its own token and speaker, so on a toy with four tokens and three speakers the frames score better than real recordings while their spread halves.

At CosyVoice's settings, guidance 0.7 and ten Euler steps on its cosine grid, no frame lands on the wrong token against 5.0 percent of recordings, the right speaker is picked 96.1 percent of the time against 64.3, and the frames spread about half as wide. CosyVoice's Table 8 shows generated speech beating recordings on real data too, at a speaker similarity of 74.30 against 69.67. Set guidance to 0 and the scores fall back toward the recordings'. On this toy ten uniform steps track the exact flow more closely than the cosine grid, 0.080 against 0.116; the paper's reason for the grid, a harder start for the network, needs a learned network to test.

Where the rebuild has to land

CosyVoice's Table 7 puts its tiny LibriTTS model at 4.76 percent WER with the released tokenizers and 3.93 with English ones, and the project is done when its own tokenizer lands within 1 point of WER and 2 of similarity of the second.

The tiny model's similarity stays at 67.85 from Exp-1 to Exp-3 while WER falls from 7.41 to 3.93, as phones and HuBERT tokens give way to English BPE and supervised English tokens. The recordings score 3.01 percent under the same scorer, so the target sits less than a point above the scorer's own error on real speech. Exp-4, the checkpoint the project reaches first with the released tokenizers, already sits just inside the box, at 0.83 points of WER and 1.91 of similarity from Exp-3, so the tolerances alone cannot tell the two tokenizers apart.

Sub-problem
Language model with flow-matching acoustic decoder engineering
Built on
CosyVoice, arXiv 2407.05407, Table 7's tiny LibriTTS model as the number to match, with FunAudioLLM/CosyVoice-300M's speech_tokenizer_v1.onnx, campplus.onnx, hift.pt and cosyvoice.yaml, LibriTTS and LibriSpeech from OpenSLR, and ESPnet's LibriSpeech recipe for the tokenizer
Time and compute
The paper gives 50 epochs on four V100s and no hours. Estimate a day each for the language model and the flow model on one A100 plus feature extraction, about 3 A100-days to the Exp-4 checkpoint, then 4 to 8 more for the ESPnet tokenizer and the retrain [T3], one GPU at a time on SLURM or Modal
Runs on
one A100 or any 24 GB card with patience

TeachesA second modality end to end: a speech tokenizer, alignment between a 50 Hz token rate and an 86 Hz frame rate, a frozen vocoder, and the two scores speech papers report

  • keep opencosyvoice.yaml from CosyVoice-300MThe mel recipe and every model size are here and nowhere else

Next steps after this one 3
  1. Make the flow decoder streaming with CosyVoice 2's chunk-aware causal masks and report time to first audio against WER at several chunk sizes
  2. Replace the Euler sampler with X-Pred MeanFlow's few-step decoder from ISCSLP 2026 and measure what the faster first packet costs in WER
  3. Retrain on LibriTTS-R, the restored corpus Nanospeech uses, to separate data quality from architecture in the gap to the recordings

  • 2024-10-31releasePhysical Intelligence releases pi0 with a flow-matching action expert on a vision-language model.Made the flow-matching action expert the robot policy design, adopted at NVIDIA, Boston Dynamics and ByteDance, and set the agenda for RL on flow policies.
  • 2024-10-31releaseDecart and Etched release Oasis, a real-time diffusion world model.

  • 2024-05-08paperAlphaFold 3 replaces its structure module with a diffusion module.

  • 2024-02paperDiscrete flow models on CTMCs co-design protein sequence and structure.

  • 2023-03-29paperDiffusion Schrodinger Bridge Matching replaces IPF solvers.
  • 2023-03-07paperDiffusion Policy makes conditional denoising of action sequences a robot policy class.
  • 2023-03-02paperConsistency models map any trajectory point to its endpoint for one-step generation.
  • 2022-10-06paperFlow matching trains continuous normalizing flows by regressing a velocity along chosen probability paths.With rectified flow and stochastic interpolants in the same month, it replaced simulation-based training with regression and opened arbitrary sources, couplings, manifolds and discrete spaces.
  • 2022-09-30paperStochastic interpolants build flows between any two densities with a quadratic loss.
  • 2022-09-07paperRectified flow regresses a velocity onto straight lines between coupled noise and data.
  • 2022-05paperDiffuser makes planning and sampling from a trajectory model nearly the same act.
  • 2021-11-18paperPeluchetti's ICLR 2022 submission argues the time-reversal argument behind denoising diffusion is unnecessary and builds generators from mixtures of diffusion bridges, the essay's opening beat.
  • 2021-11paperThe Path Integral Sampler casts sampling an unnormalized density as stochastic optimal control.
  • 2021-06paperDiffusion Schrodinger Bridge brings IPF with score networks into generative modeling.
  • 2020-11paperScore-based SDEs show each diffusion model contains a deterministic probability-flow ODE.
  • 2020-06paperDDPM makes diffusion competitive on images.
  • 2019-05paperThe Levenshtein Transformer generates text by insertions and deletions, the ancestor Edit Flows descend from.
  • 2019-02paperWaddington-OT applies optimal transport to single-cell snapshots.
  • 2019paperBoltzmann generators, published in Science after a December 2018 preprint, train flows to sample molecular equilibrium states.
  • 2018-10paperFFJORD trains free-form continuous normalizing flows by maximum likelihood, integrating an ODE at each training step, the method flow matching later retired.
  • 2018-06paperNeural ODEs introduce continuous normalizing flows trained with the adjoint method.
  • 2015-09paperMPPI makes the sampler the controller, with path-integral weights on GPU rollouts.
  • 2015-03paperDiffusion probabilistic models learn to reverse a fixed noising chain.
  • 2013-10paperUria, Murray and Larochelle introduce order-agnostic autoregression, which masked diffusion was later shown to equal.
  • 2010-03paperTabak and Vanden-Eijnden compose maps that push data toward a Gaussian, an early normalizing-flow formulation.
  • 2010paperRelative entropy policy search gives RL the exponential reweighting that later tilts generators.
  • 2009paperTodorov's linearly solvable control makes the optimal transition a reweighted passive one.
  • 2005paperKappen's path integral control, built on Fleming's log transform, linearizes the HJB equation under matched noise, with the preprint dated November 2004.
  • 2000paperBenamou and Brenier write optimal transport as the kinetic energy of a velocity field.
  • 1997paperMcCann's displacement interpolation, the term flow matching borrowed for its straight conditional paths.
  • 1991paperDai Pra shows Schrodinger bridges solve a stochastic optimal control problem.
  • 1988paperFollmer recasts the Schrodinger problem as entropy minimization over path measures.
  • 1986paperGyongy's mimicking theorem gives the conditional-to-marginal step inside flow matching.
  • 1982paperAnderson shows a reversed diffusion is a diffusion whose drift involves the score.
  • 1977paperFleming brings the logarithmic transform into control theory, linearizing a class of nonlinear control problems.
  • 1966paperNelson's stochastic mechanics splits a diffusion's velocity into current and osmotic parts, which this run reads, from a 1998 restatement, as the probability-flow velocity and the score-times-diffusion term.
  • 1957paperDoob formalizes conditioning a process on its endpoint, the h-transform behind bridge matching, guidance and pinned-path regression.
  • 1937paperKolmogorov's work on time reversibility, which the 2021 translators of Schrodinger's 1931 paper say that paper shaped.
  • 1932paperEsscher introduces exponential tilting to approximate the tail of an insurance claims distribution.
  • 1931-03paperSchrodinger poses the most likely evolution of a gas between two observed states, the Schrodinger bridge.
  • 1781paperMonge poses the problem of moving a mass distribution at least cost.

All counts come from sources.md. The corrected, downgraded, and removed figures are the tally at the top of that file, the same totals run.json records, so 205 claims failed verification as drafted. The people and codebase files, which this page leaves out, account for 42 of the corrections and 1 of the downgrades.

The contested figure counts the 46 entries in the file's Contested section. Its tally table gives 43, because the README scope lists six disagreements where its tally counts two, and avenues 01 to 04 list ten where theirs counts eleven.

The couldn't-verify figure counts the section's 60 entries. Several bundle many figures, and the avenue 08 entry alone names 14 that were not re-read, so the count of single unverified facts is higher.

Tier counts read the tier markers on the 528 checked entries, table rows and ledger entries, in the file's claims section, and an entry can carry two tiers. The 206 with no tier include the title checks and every entry in the people and codebase ledgers. No checked entry rests on a T3 guess, while each avenue's fifteen-year market line is T3 by construction and sits outside what a check can confirm.
